1:
The chapter opens on a scene of national grief, and the witnesses gather first around the people's response to Ezra's public agony. The reformed John Gill notes the plain occasion: Ezra had prayed and confessed the sins of the people in supplication, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, with many tears. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley pictures how the report spread — the account of his grief, and the public expressions of it in the court before the temple, being in an instant dispersed over all the city, brought a great company together, a happy proof of the influence the example of great ones may have upon their inferiors.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers longest on the good impressions made. No sooner was it noised abroad that their new governor, in whom they so rejoiced, was himself in grief, and to so great a degree, for them and their sin, than a very great congregation assembled to see the matter and to mingle their tears with his. Our weeping for other people's sins, Henry observes, may set those weeping for themselves who would otherwise remain senseless and remorseless; and so it proved here, for men, women, and children wept very sore. He calls the place a Bochim, a place of weepers, where at first, as among Job's friends, there seems to have fallen a profound silence, until Shechaniah broke it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same tears through the lens of dread: the people were deeply affected at the thought of God's displeasure, which they justly feared was about to light upon them because of their transgressions, and so they wept very sore. The witnesses do not divide; they weave a single portrait of a reformation begun not in cold resolve but in shared sorrow. Henry draws the pastoral moral that governs the whole chapter — where sin is thus seen and lamented, and good steps are taken toward a reformation, even sinners ought to be encouraged. The governor's private humiliation has become the congregation's public repentance, and the flood of tears that opens the chapter is, in the witnesses' reading, the first token that God will not abandon a people who can still be brought to weep for their sin.
2:
Shechaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, rises out of the weeping assembly to speak the first constructive word — "we have trespassed against our God, and have taken strange wives of the people of the land: yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set his confession in its exact terms and take pains over his identity: this Shechaniah of the sons of Elam is not the descendant of Zattu named at Ezra 8:5, and his father Jehiel is not, in their judgment, the same man as the Jehiel who appears in the register at v.26. His words "we have brought home strange wives" become the theme of all that follows.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the courage of the speaker. Adam Clarke observes that Shechaniah speaks in the name of the people, not confessing himself culpable, for he is not found in the following list — a form of speech like that of James 3:9, where with the tongue "we curse men"; and the "hope" he names is miqveh, an expectation of pardon, for the people were convinced of the evil and deeply penitent. John Wesley notes that he says "we" in the name of the whole people and their families, ranking himself among trespassers though his own name is absent from the catalogue; there we find rather his father Jehiel and five other sons of his grandfather Elam. It was therefore, Wesley judges, an evidence of great courage and a good conscience that he durst so freely discharge his duty, honouring God above his nearest and dearest relations.

The reformed John Gill adds only that Shechaniah seems to have been one of those who had lately come up with Ezra from Babylon, a chief man among the people, on whom Ezra could lean for support. The witnesses converge on the shape of the moment: the confession is frank and unqualified — the matter too plain to be denied and too bad to be excused — yet it does not end in despair. Its second clause opens a door, for the hope Shechaniah proclaims is grounded not in the innocence of Israel but in the mercy of the God against whom they have sinned. One penitent voice turns a silent flood of tears into the first step of reformation.
3:
Shechaniah moves from confession to remedy: "now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all the wives, and such as are born of them, according to the counsel of my lord, and of those that tremble at the commandment of our God." The reformed John Gill reads the proposal as a renewal — that the assembly should bind itself afresh to God by solemn promise and oath, unanimously agreeing to redress the wrong. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the sense of the whole clause: a covenant to put away the strange wives and the children born of them, made in accordance with the counsel of Ezra and of those who fear the commandment of God — the very company described as trembling at the word at Ezra 9:4 — that all might be done according to the law.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the Hebrew idiom for making the covenant, nichrath berith, literally to cut or divide a covenant sacrifice, and refers the reader to the ancient rite of passing between the divided beasts at Genesis 15:10. The pledge, that is, is no light resolution but a bond sealed with the gravest of forms. John Wesley turns to the tenderest point in the proposal, the fate of the children who are to be sent away with their mothers: these, he insists, were only to be cast out of the commonwealth of Israel, not utterly forsaken, and probably care was taken by authority that provision should be made for them.

The witnesses feel the severity and the mercy of the measure together. The command is stern — nothing less than the dissolving of unlawful unions and the sending away even of the children — and yet, on Wesley's reading, it is not merciless; and on Gill's and Keil and Delitzsch's it is not an addition of man's devising but the plain execution of the law that Ezra had already recited in his prayer. Shechaniah, who mingled more with the people than Ezra did, assures the grieving governor that the thing, hard as it is, may actually be done if they set wisely about it. What ought never to have been contracted must now, so far as possible, be undone; and true repentance, the witnesses agree, gives sin a bill of divorce and keeps nothing of what was unjustly got.
4:
"Arise; for this matter belongeth unto thee: we also will be with thee: be of good courage, and do it." The witnesses hear in Shechaniah's charge both a summons and a pledge of support. The reformed John Gill pictures the literal posture it addresses — Ezra was to rise from the ground where he lay prostrate in his grief, called up from mourning to action. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the whole verse as a rousing appeal: up, for this business concerns thee, thou art the one called to carry it out, and we will stand with thee; be strong and do it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the ground of that confidence, and it is the royal commission itself. By the decree of Artaxerxes, recited earlier at Ezra 7:23 and following, Ezra was authorized to do all that the law of God required, and every officer was commanded to be aiding and assisting to him. This is why Shechaniah can say with such assurance, "we are with you" — the people's readiness rests on a warrant that already binds the whole province to obey. The matter belongs to Ezra not by his own ambition but by the charge laid on him from the throne and, behind the throne, from God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the pastoral force of the exhortation into a single saying that has outlived its occasion: in this case weeping is good, but reforming is better. Tears had their place, and had done their work in softening the assembly; but sorrow that stops at tears is not repentance, and the time had come to translate grief into deeds. The witnesses read the verse as the turning-point where lament becomes labour. Ezra had been so overwhelmed by the corruption that he could hardly believe the people would ever part with their sin; Shechaniah, knowing them better, assures him the thing is feasible and calls him to lead it. Encouragement, the witnesses note, may rightly come even to great saints from those far their inferiors, and here a comparatively obscure man puts courage into the heart of the priest whom all Israel revered.
5:
"Then arose Ezra, and made the chief priests, the Levites, and all Israel, to swear that they should do according to this word. And they sware." The witnesses read the verse as the moment resolution hardens into a binding oath. The reformed John Gill marks the plain action — Ezra rose from the ground where he had lain, roused by Shechaniah's charge, and set at once about the work. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add a vivid detail of posture: Ezra, who through the whole of the speech had continued upon his knees, now arose, and caused the chiefs of the priests, of the Levites, and of all Israel to swear that they would act according to this word — "this word" being Shechaniah's proposal to put away the strange wives.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out why an oath was needed at all. The thing to be done was evidently contrary to the settled practice into which the people had fallen, and touched them in the dearest of their relations; and so Ezra bound them by a solemn oath to rectify the abuse, that when the first heat of feeling cooled the work might not be abandoned. An engagement sworn before God would hold when mere agreement might melt away.

The witnesses feel the wisdom of striking while the assembly was moved. The people were at that instant softened by their tears and stirred by Shechaniah's word; to bind them then, before any second thoughts or family pressures could work upon them, was to fasten the reformation while it could be fastened. The oath, moreover, was comprehensive — not the priests only, nor the leaders only, but the chief priests, the Levites, and all Israel were sworn, so that the whole community stood pledged and none could plead exemption. What Shechaniah had proposed, and the assembly had approved, is now sealed with the most sacred of bonds; and Ezra, who a moment before had lain speechless in the dust, is seen leading the nation into covenant. The witnesses take the swiftness of it as itself instructive: good resolutions are best secured at once, lest delay give the tempter room to unsettle what conviction has begun.
6:
Ezra withdraws from the open court to a private chamber to continue his mourning: "then Ezra rose up from before the house of God, and went into the chamber of Johanan the son of Eliashib: and when he came thither, he did eat no bread, nor drink water: for he mourned because of the transgression of them that had been carried away." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the abstinence as sorrow that would not be shaken off until the sin was: Ezra continued mourning, neither eating nor drinking, until something should be done to redress the grievance, teaching that sorrow for sin should be an abiding sorrow, kept up till the sin be put away. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that he retired thither to consult with the princes about the execution of their resolve, and would not be comforted till he saw something done.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the identity of the chamber's owner. Johanan the son of Eliashib cannot be the high priest Johanan of Nehemiah 12:23, for that Johanan was not the son but the grandson of Eliashib, being son of Joiada, as Nehemiah 12:10 shows; the chamber was rather one of the temple buildings named after some well-known person. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Ezra departed from before the house of God to this more retired place.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke handles the same genealogical tangle from the other side, suggesting that Johanan here may be the Jonathan of Nehemiah, son of Joiada and grandson of Eliashib, or that Johanan and Joiada were two names for one man. The witnesses do not divide over anything of weight; their small differences concern only which member of the high-priestly house lent his name to the chamber. What they agree upon is the picture of the governor's grief: having bound the people by oath, Ezra does not rest content, but shuts himself away to fast and mourn until the oath bears fruit. His sorrow is not for show but for the "transgression of them that had been carried away" — the very people God had brought back from exile now defiling the restoration with the sin that had helped bring on the captivity. Reformation, the witnesses observe, is watered by such tears as these.
7:
"And they made proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem unto all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem." The reformed John Gill notes the ordinary means employed — proclamation made by the voice of a herald, carrying the summons through every town of the province. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the resolution now carried into execution: a proclamation was sent forth (the same phrase used of Cyrus's decree elsewhere) to all the children of the captivity to assemble at Jerusalem, under the pain of a penalty to be spelled out in the next verse, and issued in the name of the princes and elders who, as heads of the community, had taken the matter in hand.

The witnesses read the step as the machinery of a real reformation, not a mere wave of feeling. It was not enough that the assembly then present had wept and sworn; the whole body of returned exiles, scattered through Judah and Benjamin, had to be gathered and confronted, and so the leaders reach for the instruments of public authority. Keil and Delitzsch note that the forfeiture of goods threatened against absentees was no wanton destruction but a devoting of the substance to the temple, after the analogy of the herem-property set apart to the LORD at Leviticus 27:28 — a penalty grave enough to compel attendance, yet turned to a sacred use rather than mere loss.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying these proceedings, marks how swiftly the wheels of reformation were set turning: they struck while the iron was hot, and lost no time. Ezra, armed by the king's grant with power to enforce his orders by penalties, sent his summons to all the children of the captivity to appear at Jerusalem within three days. The witnesses feel the seriousness of the moment in the very apparatus employed. A herald's cry, a fixed muster at the capital, a threatened forfeiture — these belong to a government in earnest, resolved that the sin should be searched out and dealt with, and not left to the slow leaking away of a general good intention. The princes and elders lend their authority; Ezra lends the king's; and behind both stands the law of God, whose command it is that the reformation means to obey.
8:
The penalty attached to the summons is now stated: "whosoever would not come within three days, according to the counsel of the princes and the elders, all his substance should be forfeited, and himself separated from the congregation of those that had been carried away." The reformed John Gill explains the tight span of three days as a means to dispatch the business quickly, forestalling any schemes to obstruct it, and guarding against the danger that those who had agreed and promised might repent and draw back before it could be done.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke read the twofold penalty together. The forfeiture of substance, Keil and Delitzsch note, is not the destruction commanded for an apostate city at Deuteronomy 13:13 and following, but its appropriation to the benefit of the temple; and the offender is separated from the congregation of the exiles. Clarke confirms both strokes: the Septuagint understood the goods to be devoted to a holy use, rendering that all his substance should be "anathematized," set apart; and the man himself is excommunicated from the Church of God and exiled from Israel. The two together — loss of property to the sanctuary and loss of standing among the people — made non-appearance ruinous.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sense of the sentence into a pointed irony: the doom of the man who would not attend on this religious occasion was that his substance should, in his stead, be for ever after appropriated to the service of religion, and he himself, for his contempt, be excluded from the honours and privileges of religion — excommunicated. The witnesses observe how the penalty fitted the offense. A man who would not come to help purge the community of its uncleanness would find himself purged out of the community instead, and his goods, which he preferred to his duty, made over to the God he had slighted. Gill's note that the three days also secured the willing against their own wavering shows the leaders' realism: they knew how quickly conviction can cool, and they closed every avenue of retreat, that the reformation might not die of delay.
9:
The muster is kept: "then all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered themselves together unto Jerusalem within three days... and all the people sat in the street of the house of God, trembling because of this matter, and for the great rain." The reformed John Gill takes "the men of Judah and Benjamin" to include such of the ten tribes as had returned and dwelt among them, and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that the phrase names not those two tribes alone — for priests, Levites, and Israelites of every stock appear in the register — but the whole returned people, so called because most were of Judah and Benjamin and all now dwelt in the land once appropriated to them.

Wesley reads the place and the weather as charged with meaning. They sat in the street next the temple, within view of it, that they might be as in God's presence and so the more awed to a faithful prosecution of the work; and the great rain they took for a token of God's displeasure against them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the season: it was the ninth month, answering to part of December, and the great rain was the winter rain of Palestine, the Septuagint rendering it "because of the winter" — the coldest and most rainy part of the year. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch locate the assembly in the open space before the temple, probably the broad place by the water-gate named at Nehemiah 8:1, and read the trembling as caused both by the gravity of the matter, whose seriousness the heavy penalty had impressed on them, and by the drenching rain in which they sat.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds a double sign in the downpour. God gave a token of his displeasure in the great rain that kept some away and distressed those who came; yet, he adds, when they wept the heavens wept too, as if to signify that though God was displeased with their sin he was well pleased with their repentance — his soul grieved for the misery of Israel, as at Judges 10:16. And the rain that fell in judgment would also make the earth fruitful, an emblem of the good fruit their repentance would bear. The witnesses leave the people shivering in the wet street before the house of God, trembling at once before the storm and before the matter that had brought them there.
10:
"And Ezra the priest stood up, and said unto them, Ye have transgressed, and have taken strange wives, to increase the trespass of Israel." The reformed John Gill sets the scene: Ezra stood up in the midst of the assembly to make his charge and to acquaint them with the reason of their being called together. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the substance of the reproof — you have brought home strange wives, and so increased the trespass of Israel — echoing the very burden of Ezra's earlier confession at Ezra 9:6 and following, where he had owned the guilt of the whole nation before God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying this address, reports what Ezra pressed upon them. He told them why he had gathered them: that since their return out of captivity they had increased the trespass of Israel by marrying strange wives, adding to their former sins a new transgression which would certainly reintroduce the very idolatry they had smarted for and which he hoped their captivity had cured. He called them together, Henry says, that they might confess their sin to God, and, having done so, declare themselves ready to do his pleasure as it should be made known — which all who truly repent will do — and particularly that they might separate themselves from all idolaters, and above all from idolatrous wives.

Keil and Delitzsch draw out the two things Ezra demanded: to give glory to God — the same call Joshua made to Achan, "make confession unto the LORD," at Joshua 7:19 — and to do his pleasure, which under the circumstances meant separation from the people of the land, that is, the dismissal of the strange wives. The witnesses feel the gravity of the moment. Ezra does not rail; he states the charge plainly and lays before them what God requires. The sin is named for what it is, an increase of Israel's trespass, a deliberate deepening of the guilt from which they had barely been delivered; and the remedy is named too, confession and separation. That the priest who had lain prostrate in grief now stands up to speak shows the reformation passing from private mourning to public reckoning, the whole assembly summoned to answer for what it had done.
11:
Ezra presses the demand home: "now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives." The reformed John Gill reads the first clause as a call to open acknowledgment — to confess their sin, to express detestation of it and repentance for it before the God of their fathers. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke deepens the note: to make confession is to acknowledge their sins before God with deep compunction of heart, and with the fullest resolution to forsake them, for confession without the purpose of amendment is empty.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend both to the demand and to the answer it drew. Ezra requires confession, obedience to God's pleasure, and separation from the people of the land and from the strange wives; and the whole assembly, they note, replied with a loud voice and therefore with firm resolve, "as thou hast said, so must we do." They observe a fine point of the Hebrew — the word "upon us," which the Vulgate wrongly drew back into the preceding clause, belongs rather with what follows, exactly as at Nehemiah 13:13: it is our duty, the people say, to act according to thy word.

The witnesses find in this verse the hinge on which the whole day turns from accusation to consent. Ezra had named the sin and the remedy; now he lays the charge on their consciences before the God of their fathers, appealing to the covenant loyalty they had inherited and betrayed. The order he presses is instructive to the witnesses: first confession, the honest owning of the wrong, then the doing of God's pleasure, and finally the concrete separation that gives repentance its proof. To confess and yet keep the strange wives would be to mock the confession; the separation is the confession made visible. And the strength of the people's reply, uttered with one loud voice, shows the assembly not cowed into a sullen compliance but roused to a hearty resolve — a whole congregation answering that what their governor has said, they are bound before God to do.
12:
"Then all the congregation answered and said with a loud voice, As thou hast said, so must we do." The reformed John Gill hears in the loud voice both audibility and unanimity — they spoke up that all might hear, and to show themselves willing and ready to comply with what had been proposed. The consent is not grudging but full-throated: the whole congregation, with one voice, ratifies the hard measure their governor has laid upon them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke weighs what that consent cost, and does not soften it. They all resolved to do what Ezra commanded, and they did put away their wives, even those by whom they had children, as the register's close at v.44 records — a great hardship, Clarke owns, upon the women and the children. By the Jewish law such marriages were null and void; yet since the women had not known these laws, their case was deplorable. Clarke will not let humanity be forgotten in zeal: we may take it for granted, he says, that each received a portion according to her husband's circumstances, and that neither wives nor children were turned away destitute, for humanity must have dictated as much, and no law of God is contrary to humanity.

Yet Clarke adds a sober doubt about how thorough or lasting the reform proved. There is some room to question, he observes, whether they finally put the strange wives away, for several years later Nehemiah found Jews that had married wives of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab, as at Nehemiah 13:23; and if these were not the very same women, at least the same offense had crept back. The witnesses thus hold together the fervor of the moment and the frailty of the human material. The congregation's loud "so must we do" is a genuine and costly act of obedience, sealing the reformation with a public vote; and yet the shadow of the later relapse falls even here, reminding the reader that a sin so deeply rooted in the affections is more easily condemned in a great assembly than kept out of the household ever after.
13:
The people's consent is real, but they plead the impossibility of settling every case on the spot: "but the people are many, and it is a time of much rain, and we are not able to stand without, neither is this a work of one day or two: for we are many that have transgressed in this thing." The reformed John Gill reads the first clause plainly — the people are many who have been guilty of this evil, too many to be dealt with in a single sitting. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the four grounds the assembly urges: the gathering is very large; it is the season of heavy rains; there is no power to stand and remain in the open air until the business is discharged; and the matter is not the work of one day or of two, for the transgressors are many.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry commends the wisdom of the proposal that grows out of this plea. It was agreed, he notes, that the affair should not be carried on in a popular assembly, nor rushed through all at once, but referred to a standing court that could receive the complaints and hear and determine them at leisure. The delinquents were many, and it would take time to discover and examine them; hard cases would arise that could not be adjudged without debate and deliberation. Better, then, to dismiss the shivering crowd and let the work proceed in order.

The witnesses admire the sober realism of the moment. Zeal untempered by prudence might have insisted on finishing everything then and there, in the cold and the wet, with hundreds of tangled cases jostling for a hearing; but the people, and Ezra with them, see that a reformation done in a hurry would be done by halves. Henry's maxim presides over the scene — that which is hastily resolved on seldom proves lasting. The very confession that they are "many that have transgressed" is at once an admission of how far the corruption had spread and a plea for the deliberate method that alone could search it out fairly. The assembly does not use its numbers or the storm as an excuse to escape; it asks only for time and order, that the thing may be done thoroughly and hold.
14:
The assembly proposes an orderly procedure: "let now our rulers of all the congregation stand, and let all them which have taken strange wives in our cities come at appointed times, and with them the elders of every city, and the judges thereof, until the fierce wrath of our God for this matter be turned from us." The reformed John Gill takes "our rulers" to mean the great court of judicature at Jerusalem — the sanhedrim, as he calls it — which was to be constituted and to sit as a standing tribunal for the affair, others assisting. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way: let the great council be settled and meet to determine all the particular causes, and let the local elders and judges attend, as those best able to inform the council of the quality of the persons and all the matters of fact and circumstance — the business to continue until the thing be done and God's wrath thereby removed.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spell out the mechanism. Let the rulers stand for the whole congregation, acting as its judicial authority; and let all who in any of the cities had brought home strange wives come before them at appointed times, each bringing the elders and judges of his own city, until the fierce wrath of God should be turned away — for so long, that is, as this matter should last. The cases were too many for the whole assembly to handle; so the transgressors were to appear district by district before the central court, each supported by the local officers who knew the facts.

The witnesses see in the plan a model of grave and deliberate justice. Rather than a mob settling the fate of families in a rainswept square, the reformation is committed to a properly constituted tribunal, before which each accused man is brought in his turn, with the officers of his own city to testify. The motive is expressly religious: the whole labour is undertaken "until the fierce wrath of our God be turned from us," the people convinced that until the sin is purged the anger it has kindled hangs over the community. Order and reverence, the witnesses note, walk together here — the machinery of a court set up not for its own sake but that God's displeasure might be appeased and the returned nation cleansed of the defilement it had contracted.
15:
"Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them." The witnesses openly divide over whether these four men were the managers of the reform or its opponents. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley take them as those appointed to conduct the business: Jonathan and Jahaziah were employed to see the affair conducted in the manner proposed — to ensure that the magistrates of every city brought forward the delinquents in their turns, to keep exact account of the whole transaction, and to prepare the causes for the judges — and Meshullam and Shabbethai, being Levites, helped them, that in any matter of doubt the persons concerned might be rightly informed.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse the opposite way. The word rendered "only" or "nevertheless" introduces a qualification, they argue, to the report that the whole assembly had resolved on the measure: notwithstanding that unanimous vote, Jonathan and Jahaziah stood up against it, supported by the two Levites, though without being able to carry their opposition. The Hebrew phrase, they say, means to stand up against a thing, as elsewhere at 2 Chronicles 20:23; and this is the reading of Rabbi Solomon and of Lightfoot, over against the older expositors and the Vulgate's steterunt super hoc, "they stood over this matter," which would make them its overseers, and the still weaker gloss that they were appointed to it. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical, fairly records both senses, noting that Dr. Lightfoot gives the contrary reading — that the four stood against the thing, or against this way of proceeding — and owning it strange if so great a work met with no opposition at all.

So the debate is real and turns on a single ambiguous verb: were Jonathan, Jahaziah, and their two Levite helpers the trusted commissioners who organized the divorces, or dissenters who resisted them and were overruled? Henry, characteristically, holds the question open. The witnesses agree only on the smaller points — that four named men are singled out, two of them Levites, and that the reformation went forward whether they furthered it or fought it. Whichever way the verb is pressed, the work was not stopped; the machinery of the court was set in motion, and the examination of the guilty began.
16:
"And the children of the captivity did so. And Ezra the priest, with certain chief of the fathers, after the house of their fathers, and all of them by their names, were separated, and sat down in the first day of the tenth month to examine the matter." The reformed John Gill notes the plain obedience of the opening clause — the children of the captivity did as had been agreed, and set about putting away their strange wives. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the commission that was formed: Ezra, together with certain heads of fathers' houses, chosen after their houses and each designated by name, was set apart, and they sat down on the first day of the tenth month to go into the matter case by case.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the word "separated" of the commissioners themselves — they sequestered themselves from all other business and gave themselves wholly to this, that the work might have their undivided attention. The examination, in other words, was entrusted to a picked body of named men who cleared their hands of everything else to sit as a court, beginning their labours a bare ten days or so after the great assembly in the rain.

The witnesses feel the orderliness and gravity of the arrangement. This was to be no rough-and-ready purge but a judicial inquiry, conducted by responsible heads of houses selected by name and given over entirely to the task; and it was Ezra who presided, though he would do nothing without their concurrence, so that the reformation rested neither on one man's zeal alone nor on the shifting mood of a crowd. That the members "sat down" to examine the matter marks the sober, deliberate temper the previous verses had called for — men taking their seats as a tribunal, prepared to hear each accused person, to sift the circumstances of every marriage, and to determine each case on its merits. The first day of the tenth month opens a session that will run, as the next verse shows, through the depth of winter, the commissioners patiently working through the long roll of the guilty while the rest of the people returned to their towns to await their summons.
17:
"And they made an end with all the men that had taken strange wives by the first day of the first month." The reformed John Gill reads the verse as the record of a completed labour — they finished their inquiry and examination of all such men, bringing the whole business to a conclusion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke counts the span it took: from the first day of the tenth month to the first day of the first month is three whole months, so that the commissioners were a full quarter of a year examining this affair and making the separations which the law required.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar of "they made an end with all." The phrase, they explain, means to make an end with the men who had brought home strange wives — to finish dealing with them — rather than, as some would have it, to make an end "in every place"; the idiom is that of finishing a matter, as at Genesis 44:12, where the search is completed. The court did not merely disperse the crowd; it worked steadily through the entire roll until every case had been heard and settled.

The witnesses draw from the three months both a lesson in diligence and a hint of the care the trials demanded. The commissioners, Matthew Henry had observed of these same proceedings, must have sat closely and minded their business, else they could never have dispatched so many causes in so short a time; yet three months for the number involved shows the work was not hurried. Each man impeached was, we may suppose, fairly asked what he could say for himself, and — if the pattern of the law held — a wife who had come over to the worship of Israel need not be put away, so that every case had to be weighed on its facts. The witnesses leave the reader with a picture of patient, unglamorous justice: a tribunal sitting through the winter and into the new year, refusing both to rush the guilty out of a hearing and to let the matter drag unresolved, until at last, on the first day of the first month, the long reckoning was brought to its end.
18:
The register of the guilty opens, fittingly and shamefully, with the priests: "and among the sons of the priests there were found that had taken strange wives... of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren; Maaseiah, and Eliezer, and Jarib, and Gedaliah." The reformed John Gill fixes on the scandal that the list should begin here at all — it need not be wondered that the evil spread among the people, when those who understood the law, and should have taught it, set such an example. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify the four names as sons and brethren of the high priest Jeshua the son of Jozadak, who had returned with Zerubbabel; the "brethren" being, from Ezra 2:36, of the house of Jedaiah, and so distant cousins of the high priest. These gave their hands, that is, bound themselves by the striking of hands, to put away their wives and to be severed from the congregation, and, being guilty, to bring a ram of the flock as a trespass-offering.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the guilt of the priesthood most heavily. Many of the priests, he notes, nay of the very family of Jeshua the high priest, were found in this trespass, though the law had specially guarded the honour of their marriages, requiring that being holy themselves they should not marry the profane, as at Leviticus 21:7. Those who should have taught others the law broke it themselves, and by their example emboldened others to do the like. Yet Henry credits their repentance: having lost their innocency, they did well to recant, promising under their hand to put away their strange wives, and taking the appointed way of pardon by bringing the ram prescribed for a trespass-offering at Leviticus 6:6, so owning their guilt and its desert and suing humbly for forgiveness.

The witnesses read the priestly names as at once the sharpest reproach and a genuine example of penitence. That the reformation should have to begin with the sons of the high priest measures how deep the corruption had gone; that they submitted first, pledging their hands and bringing their guilt-offering, gives the rest of the guilty a pattern to follow. The men whose office was to make atonement for others must here bring a sacrifice for themselves, confessing before all Israel that they too had defiled the holy seed.
19:
"And they gave their hands that they would put away their wives; and being guilty, they offered a ram of the flock for their trespass." The reformed John Gill reads the gesture as both promise and performance — they gave their hands, engaging to do it, and actually did put away their wives. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains the giving of the hand as the most solemn of pledges: they bound themselves in the fullest manner to do as the rest of the delinquents had done, and made acknowledgment of their iniquity to God, each offering a ram for a trespass-offering, so that repentance was sealed both by a public bond and by a sacrifice.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, taking the following names together, use this verse to open the wider muster of the guilty clergy. After the sons of Jeshua come the other priestly houses — the sons of Immer, of Harim, and of Pashur — and then the Levites, of whom six are named without their houses, but who are known from Ezra 2:40 to be of the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel. Among them Kelaiah is noted to be the same as Kelita, the name he bears at Nehemiah 8:7 and again at Nehemiah 10:11, where a Jozabad of this company likewise reappears; men, that is, who would afterward stand among the teachers and covenanters of Nehemiah's day.

The witnesses find in the pledged hand and the offered ram the very form of true repentance the whole chapter has been urging. The hand given is the will bound: what has been promised before God and the congregation cannot lightly be recalled. The ram brought for a trespass-offering is the confession that the sin deserved wrath and that atonement must be sought, not presumed. And Keil and Delitzsch's tracing of these Levites into the later record is quietly hopeful — several of the very men here shamed as offenders are found, a generation on, among those who read the law to the people and sealed the covenant, so that the discipline they submitted to did not crush them but restored them to honourable service. Repentance owned and atoned for, the witnesses observe, is not the end of a man but often the making of him.
44:
The book ends on its sober tally: "all these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children." The reformed John Gill closes the count at about a hundred and thirteen men in all — priests, Levites, singers, porters, and laymen together — found in the trespass and now parted from their foreign wives. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the closing clause, that only some had children, as implying that most of the wives were barren; and this, he judges, came to pass by God's special providence, to manifest his displeasure against such matches, and that the putting of them away might not be encumbered with too many difficulties.

Wesley presses on to the book's abiding lesson. One would think this grievance now thoroughly removed, he says, yet we meet with it again in Nehemiah's day at Nehemiah 13:23, for such corruptions are easily and insensibly brought in, though not easily purged out. The best reformers, he owns, can but do their endeavour; it is only the Redeemer himself who, when he comes to Zion, will effectually turn away ungodliness from Jacob — the promise of Romans 11:26. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical, sounds the same double note: the recurrence of the evil in Nehemiah 13 and again in Malachi 2:11 shows how imperfect the best human reformation must be, so that our hope rests not in Ezra's court but in Christ, whose blood alone takes away guilt and who alone can turn ungodliness from Jacob.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke dwells on the rigour with which the law was here executed, and passes on a curious tradition. According to a passage in Justin Martyr's dialogue with Trypho, Ezra on this occasion offered a paschal lamb and told the people that this passover was their Saviour and their refuge — words which, Justin alleges, the Jews afterward struck out of the book of Ezra through their enmity to Christ. Clarke reports the tale for what it is worth, and notes that in the Hebrew Ezra and Nehemiah were reckoned but one book. The witnesses close the register, and with it the book, on a chastened hope: a real reformation truly accomplished, a hundred and thirteen households purged of the strange thing, yet the seed of relapse still in the soil, and the eye lifted past every human purging to the Redeemer who alone makes an end of sin.
24:
The register passes from the priests and Levites to the lesser ministers of the temple — "of the singers also; Eliashib: and of the porters; Shallum, and Telem, and Uri." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the tally: of the singers one name is given, Eliashib, and of the porters three, Shallum, Telem, and Uri; and reckoning these together with the six Levites already named, there are ten Levites in all found in the trespass. They compare the classes to the returning musicians and gatekeepers enrolled at Ezra 2:41 and following, the same orders of temple servants now caught up in the same sin.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, glancing back over the register, marks the careful gradation of its classes — the priests of v.18, the Levites of v.23, and the singers of this verse — each order set down in its own rank before the historian turns to the laity of Israel. The list is no random heap of names but a descent through the ministering household of God, from the sons of the high priest down to the doorkeepers who guarded the temple gates.

The witnesses feel the sober justice of so ordered a roll. The men who led the worship of the restored community — the Levite Eliashib who lifted the song in the courts, the porters who kept the thresholds of the LORD's house — were not passed over because their office was near to holy things; rather their nearness made their fault the plainer, and their names are entered with the rest. Only ten Levites in all, singers and porters included, were found guilty, a small number set against the priests above them and the many laymen to follow; yet the register spares not even these few. That the keepers of the gate should themselves have let the strange thing in, and the leaders of praise have needed to put away what dishonoured their song, is the chapter's warning carried into the very sanctuary: the discipline that begins at the altar reaches to the doorway, and no servant of the house, however humble his charge, stands outside the reckoning.
25:
With the ministers of the temple accounted for, the register turns to the mass of the laity — "moreover of Israel: of the sons of Parosh; Ramiah, and Jeziah, and Malchiah, and Miamin, and Eleazar, and Malchijah, and Benaiah." The wesleyan-arminian voices explain the heading. Adam Clarke, following Calmet, takes "of Israel" to mean simple Israelites, so named to distinguish them from the priests, Levites, and singers already enumerated; and John Wesley likewise reads it of the people of Israel as distinguished from the priests and Levites hitherto named. The word marks the great turn in the list, from the ministering orders to the common body of the returned nation.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the reckoning behind the section. Of Israel, as distinguished from priests and Levites — that is, of the laity — there are given in all some eighty-six names, belonging to ten of the great families that had come back with Zerubbabel, the sons of Parosh standing first, as they stand at the head of the lay houses in the return at Ezra 2:3. These clans are the same well-known stocks whose numbers were counted at the first return, now furnishing their quota of offenders in the matter of the strange wives.

The witnesses observe how the register, having begun with the holiest, now spreads to the whole community, sparing no rank. Keil and Delitzsch note in passing a difficulty that will trouble the reading of the section — the house of Bani appears to be named twice over, and one of the two occurrences is very likely a copyist's error for another family — a caution that the long roll, faithfully as it was kept, bears the ordinary marks of ancient transcription. But the substance stands clear: the same lay families that had rejoiced to return from Babylon are here numbered among the guilty, the sons of Parosh at their head. The historian, the witnesses feel, keeps the count deliberately, that the reader may see how far the corruption had reached — not into the priesthood alone, but through clan after clan of ordinary Israel, each named that its shame and its repentance alike might stand on record.
26:
The lay register runs on through family after family — "and of the sons of Elam; Mattaniah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, and Abdi, and Jeremoth, and Eliah" — and then through the sons of Zattu, Bebai, Bani, Pahath-moab, Harim, Hashum, and Nebo, until the whole company is summed at the chapter's close. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, surveying the block, note that these ten lay houses correspond to the great families of the return, and mark again the textual puzzle running through it: the sons of Bani are named twice, and where every other house yields four, six, seven, or eight offenders, the second Bani carries an improbable twenty-seven names, so that one of the two headings is almost certainly a scribe's slip — perhaps, as some suppose, Bigvai standing originally in its place.

Upon the first-named house here, the sons of Elam, the witnesses fasten a striking connection, and divide over it. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley had already observed that the Jehiel named among these guilty sons of Elam was the very father of Shechaniah, who at v.2 rose to propose the whole reformation; so that the man who first cried "we have trespassed" is found to have accused his own father and his father's house, five other sons of Elam being here in the list — an evidence, Wesley urged, of his great courage and good conscience in honouring God above his nearest kin. Keil and Delitzsch, however, expressly deny the identification, holding that the Jehiel who was Shechaniah's father is not the same man as the Jehiel whose name occurs in this verse.

The witnesses thus leave a genuine question hanging over the roll of Elam: whether the reformer's own father stands here among the condemned, or only a namesake. Wesley finds in the identity the noblest proof of Shechaniah's integrity; Keil and Delitzsch, weighing the names more cautiously, keep the two apart. Beyond that dispute the witnesses agree on the register's plain testimony — clan after clan of ordinary Israel, the same stocks that had returned from exile, numbered here among the guilty. The list keeps each name, whether great or obscure, that the extent of the corruption and the completeness of the reckoning might alike be seen; and the historian's very care over a doubtful heading and a possible copyist's error shows how faithfully the record was preserved.
20:
The roll of guilty priests continues beyond the high-priestly house of Jeshua into the other great priestly families — "and of the sons of Immer; Hanani, and Zebadiah." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, handling the priestly register as a whole, set these names in their order among the courses that had returned from Babylon. The sons of Immer stand here with the sons of Harim and of Pashur, the same priestly houses enrolled among the returning exiles at Ezra 2:37 and following; and like the sons of Jeshua before them, these too, being guilty, gave their hands to put away their wives and brought a ram of the flock for a trespass-offering, the whole company of implicated priests thus dealt with on one footing.

The reformed John Gill's observation upon the priests governs the reading of every such name: it need not be wondered that the evil spread among the people, when those who understood the law and should have taught it were themselves ensnared. That the corruption reached not one priestly house only but Immer, Harim, and Pashur alike shows how widely the leaven had worked through the very order set apart to guard the holiness of Israel. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry pressed the same weight — that they whose office was to instruct others in the law had broken it, and by their example emboldened the people to do likewise, so that their names are written here to their lasting reproach.

Yet the witnesses find in the bare list more than reproach. Each of these houses, having sinned, submitted; the sons of Immer no less than the sons of Jeshua pledged their hands and brought their guilt-offering, so that the whole priesthood, from the high priest's own kin down through the several courses, is seen bowing to the same discipline and seeking the same atonement. The register keeps the count exact and impartial, sparing neither the greatest house nor the least. Hanani and Zebadiah of the sons of Immer stand for the truth the chapter presses everywhere — that no rank or office exempts a man from the reckoning, and that the sin which must be confessed by the people must first be confessed, and first put away, by the priests who led them into it.
38:
Deep in the long roll of lay offenders stand three more names — "and Bani, and Binnui, Shimei" — belonging to the troubled second listing of the sons of Bani that runs through the heart of the register. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat these names within the textual difficulty they had already flagged. The house of Bani, they observe, is named twice in this catalogue, and while every other family yields but a handful of guilty men, the second Bani is followed by some twenty-seven names — far too many for a single clan — so that the heading is almost certainly corrupt. One of the two occurrences of "the sons of Bani" must be a copyist's error for another family, and it is likely, as has been conjectured, that Bigvai or some such house originally stood where the second Bani now appears. The names themselves, Bani and Binnui and Shimei among them, are genuine; it is only the ascription of so long a string to one father that betrays a slip in the transmission.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, reflecting on this whole catalogue of the guilty, reminds the reader why such bare names were preserved at all: they are recorded here, he says, to their perpetual reproach, that after-ages might know at what cost the holiness of Israel was guarded and how far even the returned people had fallen. Yet the same names are also, the witnesses feel, a record of repentance, for every man written here had given his hand and submitted to the discipline; the roll of shame is at once a roll of the reformed.

The witnesses thus read even this obscure fragment of the list with care. That the text should carry a manifest difficulty — a family named twice, a count too large for one house — the grammatical-historical school neither hides nor magnifies, treating it as one of the ordinary marks of a hand-copied record, to be noted honestly and left. And the moral Henry draws hovers over the least of the names: Bani, Binnui, and Shimei are not great men whose deeds fill the history, but ordinary Israelites whose one recorded act is that they had sinned in the matter of the strange wives and then put them away. Scripture keeps their names, that neither the extent of the fault nor the reality of the reckoning should ever be forgotten.
